title: Painting a concrete garage floor
subtitle: Degrease, etch, prime, and coat a concrete floor with two-part epoxy or single-pack floor paint for a hard-wearing sealed surface
excerpt: How to paint a concrete garage floor using floor paint. Covers degreasing, etching, priming if required, and applying two coats of floor paint for a durable, sealed finish.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for concrete-floor coatings.

glossaryTerms.definition: A single-pack or two-part epoxy paint formulated for concrete floors. Single-pack versions (water-based or solvent-based) are easier to apply and adequate for light-vehicle use. Two-part epoxy versions are harder, more chemical-resistant, and more durable under daily vehicle traffic.

A treatment applied to a concrete surface before painting, in which a dilute acid solution (typically phosphoric or hydrochloric acid) opens the surface pores to improve paint adhesion. The acid is applied, left to react, then neutralised and rinsed off thoroughly before painting.

content.text: A painted concrete garage floor seals the surface against oil, dust, and moisture. The approach is degrease, key the surface, and apply two coats of
. The degreasing and keying steps are where most jobs fail; the paint is the easy part.

Move everything out of the garage. Sweep and vacuum the floor. Any oil stain must be treated before painting: pour neat washing soda crystals over the stain, leave for 30 minutes, then scrub with a stiff brush and hot water. Repeat until the stain no longer darkens fresh water poured on it. If oil has soaked deeply into the concrete, a specialist concrete degreaser works better. Rinse the whole floor and allow to dry fully (at least 24 hours in mild weather).
Smooth or burnished concrete does not grip paint well.

opens the surface pores. Apply a dilute solution of phosphoric acid concrete etch (mixed to the maker's instructions) across the whole floor. It will fizz slightly on contact with the concrete. Leave for 15 minutes, then scrub with a stiff brush. Rinse with plenty of clean water, neutralise if the product requires it, and allow to dry fully before painting (at least 24 hours).

Wear protective gloves, safety glasses, and old clothing. Ventilate the garage fully by opening doors and windows. Do not allow the acid solution to contact skin. Keep a bucket of water nearby for rinsing.

Stir the paint thoroughly. Use the 50 mm brush to cut in around the edges and into any corners. Apply the main area with a 9-inch roller, working in strips away from the door. Keep the coat thin and even; a thick single coat sags and takes much longer to dry. Allow to dry fully according to the paint manufacturer's instructions (typically 4 to 6 hours for single-pack, overnight for two-part epoxy).

Apply the second coat in the same way as the first. Two coats give a durable, sealed finish. Do not park a vehicle on the floor for at least 3 days after the final coat; the paint may be touch-dry long before it reaches full hardness. For two-part epoxy, check the maker's cure schedule before subjecting the floor to vehicle weight.
Decorative flake finish: scatter vinyl colour flakes onto the wet first coat. When dry, apply a clear top coat. The result has a speckled, multi-colour look.
Anti-slip finish: stir a fine anti-slip aggregate into the topcoat before applying. This gives grip underfoot in a workshop or utility space.

attrs.symptom: Paint peels in sheets within weeks of application
attrs.cause: The surface was not degreased or etched before painting. Oil or a smooth burnished surface prevented adhesion.
attrs.fix: Strip the paint back to bare concrete, degrease thoroughly, etch, and reapply.

attrs.symptom: White powdery patches appear through the paint after a few months
attrs.cause: Efflorescence: soluble salts in the concrete migrating to the surface with moisture movement.
attrs.fix: Strip the affected area, treat with a concrete primer or sealant that blocks efflorescence, then re-coat.
